aliases: Order of the Holy Redeemer of Montjoy

imageInfo.caption: The Castle of Monfragüe above the Tagus, held from 1196 by the Order of Montjoy’s Castilian and Leonese breakaway, in a 2017 photograph; its square keep was added in the fifteenth century.
imageInfo.creator: Falk2
imageInfo.date: Photograph June 2017; castle founded in the ninth century, keep fifteenth century
imageInfo.note: A modern colour photograph of the castle on the ridge above the Tagus, now dammed as the Torrejón-Tajo reservoir. The castle was first built under Islamic rule in the ninth century; the square keep in the foreground dates from the fifteenth century, after the order’s time, according to the photographer’s record. Alfonso VIII of Castile granted Monfragüe in 1196 to the order’s knights who refused its union with the Templars, and they held it as the Order of Monfragüe until 1221. The order’s own first seat, Alfambra in Aragon, survives only as an archaeological site. It replaces an illustration of the order’s arms, a white shield with a red cross, which read as a blank white image.

sigilImageInfo.caption: A 2008 digital drawing of the half-red, half-white eight-pointed cross often shown for the order; the design is not medieval.
sigilImageInfo.creator: Life of Riley
sigilImageInfo.note: Commons describes it as the alleged cross of the order. The medieval emblem recorded for Montjoy is a red cross patée, sometimes white; the eight-pointed half-and-half form resembles the Maltese cross and was drawn later.

summary: The Order of Montjoy was a small military order founded in 1173–1174 at Alfambra, in the Kingdom of Aragon, by Rodrigo Álvarez de Sarria, a Leonese count and former knight of Santiago, and named after Montjoie outside Jerusalem. Its eastern knights died at Hattin in 1187. In 1188 Alfonso II of Aragon merged it into his Hospital of the Holy Redeemer at Teruel, which passed to the Templars in 1196, while a Castilian and Leonese breakaway at Monfragüe joined Calatrava in 1221.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: The Order of Montjoy, Monte Gaudio in Spanish, was a small military order founded in the Kingdom of Aragon in 1173–1174 by Rodrigo Álvarez de Sarria, a count from Galicia in the Kingdom of León who had been a knight of the Order of Santiago. For its first years it was known simply as the Order of Alfambra, after the castle north of Teruel that Alfonso II of Aragon gave it in July 1174 in return for holding his frontier against Muslim Valencia.

The name came a few years later. On a pilgrimage in 1176–1177 Rodrigo acquired land in the Kingdom of Jerusalem, including Montjoie, the hill outside Jerusalem from which pilgrims caught their first sight of the city. The order never grew large on either front, and within fifteen years of its foundation it had lost its independence.

contentSections.title: Santiago, Alfambra and Montjoie
paragraphs: Rodrigo left Santiago because he found its discipline too lax, above all because its knights were allowed to marry, and he wanted a stricter rule modelled on the Cistercians’. The papal legate Cardinal Hyacinth, the future Pope Celestine III, gave permission, and Pope Alexander III approved the new order before 24 December 1173 on condition that it took in no former knights of Santiago and no property Santiago claimed. A papal bull of 1180 confirmed it. Unusually for an order under a Cistercian rule, it answered directly to the Holy See rather than to Cîteaux or to the Order of Calatrava.

Alfambra was its first seat, charged with the frontier south of Teruel. In the East, the lands Rodrigo received on his pilgrimage came from Raynald of Châtillon, and Baldwin IV of Jerusalem confirmed them on condition that Rodrigo and his knights fight there. The order also received smaller grants in Castile and Italy. Neither front brought it many recruits: the name Monte Gaudio appears less and less in the documents after 1180, and an attempt around 1186 to unite the order with the Knights Templar came to nothing.

contentSections.title: Hattin, Teruel and the Templars
paragraphs: The order’s knights in the East fought at the Battle of Hattin on 4 July 1187, where Saladin destroyed the army of the Kingdom of Jerusalem, and none of them survived. The fall of Jerusalem that October ended the order’s role in the Holy Land.

In 1188 Alfonso II folded the brothers of Alfambra into the Hospital of the Holy Redeemer, which he had founded at Teruel. The merged Order of the Holy Redeemer kept Alfambra’s rule and customs, added the hospital’s work of ransoming captives and caring for the needy, and received generous royal grants.

It broke apart in 1196. The brothers, unhappy with their master Fralmo of Lucca, replaced him with Rodrigo González; Fralmo took the mastership back against canon law, gave up the Cistercian rule and led the order into the Knights Templar that same year. Its houses in Aragon, Alfambra among them, passed to the Templars.

contentSections.title: The Monfragüe breakaway
paragraphs: Rodrigo González’s supporters, most of them Castilian and Leonese knights, refused the union. In 1196 Alfonso VIII of Castile granted them Monfragüe, a castle on a ridge above the Tagus in Extremadura, and they carried on there as the Order of Monfragüe until Ferdinand III of Castile joined them to the Order of Calatrava in 1221.

So the order ended three ways: its eastern knights died at Hattin, its Aragonese houses went to the Templars, and its Castilian remnant was absorbed by Calatrava. When the Templars were suppressed, Alfambra passed to the Hospitallers, and Juan Fernández de Heredia, later Grand Master of the Hospitallers at Rhodes, began his career as its commander. The Order of Montesa, founded in 1317, owed something to proposals made then to revive Montjoy.

timeline.title: Papal approval

myths.claim: Montjoy was founded in the Holy Land.
myths.reality: It was founded at Alfambra in Aragon in 1173–1174. Its land at Montjoie outside Jerusalem, which gave it its name, came on the founder’s pilgrimage in 1176–1177.
In 1188 Alfonso II of Aragon merged it into his Hospital of the Holy Redeemer at Teruel. The Templars received that order only in 1196, and a Castilian breakaway lasted at Monfragüe until 1221.

myths.claim: The half-red, half-white eight-pointed cross is its medieval emblem.
myths.reality: The medieval emblem recorded for the order is a red cross patée, sometimes white. The eight-pointed form resembles the Maltese cross and is a later drawing.
